summary: The charter of the Internet Architecture Board, a technical advisory group of the Internet Society. It describes how the IAB is formed and operates. It was replaced by RFC 1601.

plainLanguage.summary: The founding rules of the group that advises on how the Internet should be built, saying who is in it and what it does.

subtitle: The founding rules of the Internet technical advisory board.

tldr.problem: The Internet Architecture Board needed a formal charter defining its membership, governance, and responsibilities as a technical advisory group of the Internet Society.
tldr.mechanism: Establish the IAB with up to 15 individual members nominated by the IAB, Internet Society leadership, or member petition. Define the roles of the IAB chair, RFC Editor, IETF chair, and IRTF chair, with appointment and removal procedures.
tldr.outcome: The IAB charter formalizes how Internet architecture decisions are made and how the standards and RFC publication process are managed. This version was replaced by RFC 1601.

sections.title: The IAB and Its Role
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) serves as a technical advisory group to the Internet Society. It is responsible for expert oversight of Internet architecture, management of the Request for Comments (RFC) series, development and approval of Internet Standards, and providing advice to the Internet Society's Board of Trustees on technical matters.

The IAB also represents the Internet Society's interests in liaison relationships with other organizations. The Internet Society may assign additional responsibilities to the IAB as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB is the group of technical experts who advise on how to build the Internet and who publishes the standards documents (RFCs).

sections.title: Membership and Governance
sections.content:
The IAB consists of no more than 15 members serving as individuals, not as representatives of their employers. Members are nominated by the IAB itself, the President of the Internet Society, the Board of Trustees, or by petition from at least 1% of the Internet Society membership (or 150 members, whichever is larger). The Board of Trustees must approve nominations within 60 days by a three-fifths majority.

Any IAB member may be removed by the Board of Trustees with a four-fifths vote. The Board also reviews each member's contribution every three years and must explicitly reaffirm or revoke membership. Members serve on a volunteer basis, though the Internet Society may reimburse expenses or pay compensation in exceptional cases where the President and Board determine it is necessary for the welfare of the Society.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB has at most 15 members who are picked by the IAB, the Internet Society's leadership, or by members voting. They can be removed if they are not helping.

sections.title: Key Officers and Task Forces
sections.content:
The IAB members elect one of their number as chair, who has all normal duties of a chairperson and may be removed by a two-thirds vote. The chair appoints an Editor for the RFC series (the RFC Editor), who manages publication of all RFCs and may be removed by two-thirds IAB vote. If the RFC Editor is not an IAB member, they serve ex officio.

The IAB chair also appoints the chair of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), responsible for engineering standards, and the chair of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), responsible for research. Both chairpersons may be removed by two-thirds vote. The Internet Society provides secretariat support for the IAB and its task forces, subject to Board approval and available funding.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB picks a leader from among themselves. That leader appoints the RFC Editor and the heads of two task forces: IETF (for engineering) and IRTF (for research).
